To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
OPA1 mutations are found in 67% of the patients with a suspected hereditary optic atrophy.

(1) OPA1 is the most frequently mutated gene in hereditary optic neuropaths, (2) the majority of OPA1 mutations are de novo mutations, (3) the majority of the OPA3 mutations are in the same exon and in the same region of the protein, and (4) the OPA1 gene is the most frequently involved gene in hereditary autosomal dominant optic neuropathy.

(1) OPA1 mutations are the most frequent cause of hereditary optic neuropaties, and (2) molecular screening for OPA1 mutations should be performed in all cases of suspected heredity optic neuropathy, including apparently isolated cases of optic atrophies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular genetics and molecular biology of the human OPA1 gene, which is the major cause of autosomal dominant optic neuropathy.
the study of molecular defects in the OPA1 gene, which is involved in the pathogenesis of dominant optic atrophy.
the development of novel methods and tools to study the genetic and molecular bases of neurodegeneration and the application of such methods to human disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the OPA1 gene is the most common gene mutated in cases of hereditary optic neuropaths.
OPA1 is a very large gene and the most important cause of ADOA, but that it is not a simple matter of finding an OPA1 defect in a case of suspected ADOA.
the molecular screening of 980 patients with suspected hereditary optic atrophy led to the identification of a molecular defect in 45% of cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

OPA1 is an important gene for the pathogenesis of optic atrophy and that the molecular screening of OPA1 should be considered for all patients with a diagnosis of optic atrophy, even in the absence of a family background.
